method_card.title: Volume & Surface Area
steps: Name the solid and pick its formula.
Work the \(\pi\) part last, then round as asked.
Add or subtract parts for compound solids.
method_card.content:
Pick the solid, use its formula, substitute, and keep the units (cm³ for volume, cm² for area).

Cuboid \(V = lwh\). Prism \(V = \text{area} \times \text{length}\). Cylinder \(V = \pi r^2 h\). Cone \(V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\), curved SA \(= \pi r l\). Sphere \(V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), SA \(= 4\pi r^2\). Pyramid \(V = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \text{base} \times h\). A hemisphere is half a sphere.

For compound solids add or subtract simpler shapes. To find a missing length from a given volume, rearrange first.
method_card.example:
Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 4 cm and height 10 cm.

\(V = \pi \times 4^2 \times 10 = 160\pi \approx 502.7\) cm³

bronze.display: Find the volume of a cube with side length 6 cm.
bronze.hint: Multiply the side by itself three times: 6 × 6 × 6.

misconceptions.message: Stopping at 6 × 6 = 36 gives the area of one square face. A cube's volume needs the third length too: 6 × 6 × 6 = 216 cm³.

guided_steps.say: Volume of a cube is side × side × side. The side is 6 cm.
Multiply by the third side of 6.

guided_steps.done: That returns the side length 6 cm, so 216 cm³ is right.

bronze.display: A cuboid is 10 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm. Find its volume.

misconceptions.message: Adding the three lengths (10 + 4 + 3 = 17) measures edges, not the space inside. Volume multiplies them: 10 × 4 × 3 = 120 cm³.

guided_steps.say: Volume of a cuboid is length × width × height: 10 × 4 × 3.
Now multiply by the height of 3.

guided_steps.done: That returns the length 10 cm, so 120 cm³ is right.

bronze.display: A triangular prism has cross-section area 15 cm² and length 9 cm. Find its volume.
bronze.hint: Multiply the cross-section area by the length.

misconceptions.message: Using just the cross-section area (15 cm²) forgets the prism's length. Multiply by the length: 15 × 9 = 135 cm³.

guided_steps.say: Volume of a prism is cross-section area × length: 15 × 9.
Nine lots of 15 is ten lots minus one lot.

guided_steps.done: That returns the cross-section area 15 cm², so 135 cm³ is right.

bronze.display: A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume to 1 d.p.
bronze.hint: Square the radius, multiply by the height, then by π.

misconceptions.message: Using the diameter (6 cm) in place of the radius: π × 6² × 10 = 360π ≈ 1131.0 cm³. The formula needs the radius (3 cm): π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³.

guided_steps.say: Volume of a cylinder is π × r² × h. Start with r².
That is the number in front of π: 90π.

guided_steps.hint: Type 90 × π and round to one decimal place.

guided_steps.say: Check: the base circle has area π × 9 ≈ 28.3 cm², and over height 10 that is about 283 cm³, matching 282.7 cm³.

bronze.display: Find the surface area of a cube with side 5 cm.
bronze.hint: A cube has six identical faces, so find one face area and multiply by 6.

misconceptions.message: 25 cm² is the area of a single face. A cube has 6 faces, so multiply by 6: 6 × 25 = 150 cm².

guided_steps.say: A cube has 6 identical square faces. Each face is 5 × 5.
There are 6 faces, all the same.

guided_steps.done: That returns one face area, 25 cm², so 150 cm² is right.

bronze.display: A cuboid is 8 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm. Find its surface area.
bronze.hint: Find the three different face areas, add them, then double.

misconceptions.message: 24 + 16 + 6 = 46 counts each face size only once. Every face has a matching opposite, so double it: 2 × 46 = 92 cm².

guided_steps.say: A cuboid has three different face sizes, each appearing twice. Find the three areas.
These are the three different faces.

guided_steps.done: Two of each face makes the whole surface, 92 cm².

bronze.display: A cylinder has radius 4 cm and height 7 cm. Find the volume to 1 d.p.
bronze.hint: Square the radius, times the height, times π.

misconceptions.message: Using the diameter (8 cm) instead of the radius: π × 8² × 7 = 448π ≈ 1407.4 cm³. Halve it to the radius (4 cm): π × 16 × 7 = 112π ≈ 351.9 cm³.

guided_steps.say: Volume of a cylinder is π × r² × h. Start with r².
That is the number in front of π: 112π.

guided_steps.hint: Type 112 × π and round to one decimal place.

guided_steps.say: Check: base area π × 16 ≈ 50.3 cm², times height 7 ≈ 352 cm³, matching 351.9 cm³.

bronze.display: A fish tank is 40 cm × 25 cm × 30 cm. How many litres of water does it hold?
bronze.hint: Find the volume in cm³, then divide by 1000 to get litres.

misconceptions.message: The volume is 40 × 25 × 30 = 30000 cm³. Dividing by 100 gives 300, which treats a litre as 100 cm³. A litre is 1000 cm³, so divide by 1000: 30 litres.

guided_steps.say: First find the volume in cm³: length × width × height.
So the tank holds 30000 cm³.

guided_steps.pre: There are 1000 cm³ in 1 litre, so 30000 ÷ 1000 =
guided_steps.say: Now change cm³ into litres.

guided_steps.done: That returns the volume in cm³, so 30 litres is right.

silver.display: Find the volume of a sphere with radius 6 cm to 1 d.p.
silver.hint: Cube the radius, then multiply by four thirds and π.

misconceptions.message: 4π × 36 = 144π ≈ 452.4 is the surface area, not the volume. Volume cubes the radius and uses four thirds: (4/3)π × 216 = 288π ≈ 904.8 cm³.
misconceptions.note: Determinate slip: SA formula for volume.

guided_steps.say: Volume of a sphere is (4/3) × π × r³. Start with r³.
Cube means three sixes multiplied.
Now apply the four thirds.

guided_steps.hint: Type 288 × π and round to one decimal place.

silver.display: Find the volume of a cone with radius 5 cm and height 12 cm to 1 d.p.
silver.hint: Square the radius, times height, times a third, times π.

misconceptions.message: π × 25 × 12 = 300π ≈ 942.5 is a cylinder's volume. A cone is one third of that: (1/3) × 300π = 100π ≈ 314.2 cm³.

guided_steps.say: Volume of a cone is (1/3) × π × r² × h. Start with r².
That is r² × h.
A cone is a third of the matching cylinder.

guided_steps.hint: Type 100 × π and round to one decimal place.

guided_steps.say: Check: without the third it would be 300π; a third of that is 100π ≈ 314.2 cm³.

silver.display: A cylinder has volume 500 cm³ and radius 5 cm. Find the height to 1 d.p.
silver.hint: Rearrange V = πr²h to h = V ÷ (πr²).

misconceptions.message: Dividing by the radius instead of its square: 500 ÷ (5π) ≈ 31.8. The formula has r², so divide by π × 25: 500 ÷ (25π) ≈ 6.4 cm.
misconceptions.note: Determinate slip: divides by r not r².

guided_steps.say: V = π × r² × h, so rearrange to h = V ÷ (π × r²). First find π × r².

guided_steps.hint: Type π × 25 and round to two decimal places.
guided_steps.say: That is the whole base-times-π amount.

guided_steps.hint: Volume divided by the base amount.

guided_steps.say: Check: π × 25 × 6.366 = 500 exactly; rounding the height to 6.4 explains the tiny gap, so h ≈ 6.4 cm is right.

silver.display: Find the curved surface area of a cone with radius 4 cm and slant height 9 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.
silver.hint: Curved surface of a cone is π × radius × slant height.

misconceptions.message: 2π × 4 × 9 = 72π ≈ 226.2 is a cylinder's curved surface. A cone's is π × r × l with no 2: π × 4 × 9 = 36π ≈ 113.1 cm².

guided_steps.say: Curved surface area of a cone is π × r × l. Multiply r and l first.
That is the number in front of π: 36π.

guided_steps.hint: Type 36 × π and round to one decimal place.

guided_steps.pre: Check: 113.1 ÷ π, to the nearest whole number =
guided_steps.hint: Divide the answer back by π.
guided_steps.done: That returns 36, which is r × l = 4 × 9, so 113.1 cm² is right.

silver.display: Find the surface area of a sphere with radius 4 cm to 1 d.p.
silver.hint: Square the radius, then multiply by 4 and π.

misconceptions.message: π × 4² = 16π ≈ 50.3 is the area of a flat circle. A sphere's surface is 4 times that: 4π × 16 = 64π ≈ 201.1 cm².
misconceptions.note: Determinate slip: circle area, not sphere.

guided_steps.say: Surface area of a sphere is 4 × π × r². Start with r².
That is the number in front of π: 64π.

guided_steps.hint: Type 64 × π and round to one decimal place.

guided_steps.say: Check: 201.1 ÷ π ≈ 64, which is 4 × 16, so 201.1 cm² is right.

silver.display: A pyramid has square base 6 cm × 6 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume.
silver.hint: A third of base area times height.

misconceptions.message: 36 × 10 = 360 would be a prism with that base. A pyramid is one third of it: (1/3) × 360 = 120 cm³.

guided_steps.say: Volume of a pyramid is (1/3) × base area × height. Find the base area first.

guided_steps.hint: Six squared for the square base.

guided_steps.say: That is base area × height.
A pyramid is a third of that box.

guided_steps.done: That returns base area × height = 36 × 10, so 120 cm³ is right.

silver.display: A hemisphere has radius 8 cm. Find its volume to the nearest whole number.
silver.hint: A hemisphere is two thirds of πr³.

misconceptions.message: (4/3)π × 512 ≈ 2145 is a whole sphere. A hemisphere is half of that, or two thirds of πr³: (2/3)π × 512 ≈ 1072 cm³.

guided_steps.say: A hemisphere is half a sphere, so its volume is (2/3) × π × r³. Start with r³.
Cube means three eights multiplied.
Apply the two thirds.

guided_steps.pre: 341.33 × π, to the nearest whole number =

guided_steps.say: Check: a full sphere would be (4/3)π × 512 ≈ 2145 cm³; a hemisphere is half of that, ≈ 1072 cm³.

gold.display: A sphere has volume \(288\pi\) cm³. Find the radius.
gold.hint: Cancel the π, then rearrange (4/3)r³ = 288 and cube root.

misconceptions.message: Taking r³ = 288 straight from 288π ignores the four thirds. Cancel π then multiply by 3/4: r³ = 288 × 3/4 = 216, so r = 6 cm. r = ∛288 ≈ 6.6 is the slip.
misconceptions.note: Determinate slip: r = cube root of 288.

guided_steps.say: Volume of a sphere is (4/3)πr³, and here it equals 288π. The π cancels, so (4/3)r³ = 288, giving r³ = 288 × (3/4).
So r³ = 216.
Check: 6³ = 216 and (4/3) × 216 = 288, so the volume is 288π. The radius is 6 cm.

gold.display: A cone and a cylinder have the same base radius (5 cm) and the same height (12 cm). Find the difference in their volumes to 1 d.p.
gold.hint: The difference is two thirds of the cylinder's volume.

misconceptions.message: Treating the cone as a cylinder makes both 300π, so the difference looks like 0. The cone is only one third, 100π, so the difference is 300π − 100π = 200π ≈ 628.3 cm³.

guided_steps.say: Cylinder volume is πr²h; the cone is one third of it, so the difference is two thirds of the cylinder. First find r²h.
Cylinder = 300π, cone = 100π.
The gap is the cylinder minus the cone.

guided_steps.hint: Type 200 × π and round to one decimal place.

guided_steps.say: Check: cylinder = 300π, cone = 100π, difference = 200π ≈ 628.3 cm³.

gold.display: A solid hemisphere of radius 4 cm sits on top of a cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. Find the total volume to 1 d.p.
gold.hint: Add the cylinder volume and the hemisphere volume.

misconceptions.message: Adding a whole sphere instead of a hemisphere: 160π + (4/3)π × 64 = 160π + (256/3)π ≈ 770.7. A hemisphere is two thirds of πr³, giving 160π + (128/3)π ≈ 636.7 cm³.
misconceptions.note: Determinate slip: full sphere on top.

guided_steps.say: Add two volumes. Cylinder = πr²h; hemisphere = (2/3)πr³. Find each number in front of π.

guided_steps.hint: Square the radius, times the height.
guided_steps.say: Cylinder = 160π.
Hemisphere ≈ 42.67π.

guided_steps.hint: Sum the numbers in front of π.
guided_steps.say: Now combine the coefficients of π.

guided_steps.hint: Type 202.67 × π and round to one decimal place.

gold.display: A sphere has surface area \(100\pi\) cm². Find the radius.
gold.hint: Cancel the π, solve 4r² = 100, then square root.

misconceptions.message: Stopping at r² = 25 gives 25, but the question wants r. Take the square root: r = √25 = 5 cm.
misconceptions.note: Determinate slip: forgets the square root.

guided_steps.say: Surface area of a sphere is 4πr², and here it equals 100π. The π cancels, so 4r² = 100, giving r² = 100 ÷ 4.
So r² = 25.

guided_steps.done: 4 × 25 = 100, so the surface is 100π, and r = 5 cm is right.

gold.display: A frustum is formed by removing a cone of height 4 cm and radius 2 cm from a cone of height 12 cm and radius 6 cm. Find the volume of the frustum to 1 d.p.
gold.hint: Big cone volume minus small cone volume.

misconceptions.message: 144π ≈ 452.4 is just the large cone. The frustum removes the small cone (16π/3): 144π − 16π/3 = 416π/3 ≈ 435.6 cm³.

guided_steps.say: The frustum is the big cone minus the small cone. Volume of a cone is (1/3)πr²h. Find each number in front of π.
Big cone = 144π.
Small cone ≈ 5.33π.
The frustum is what is left after removing the tip.

guided_steps.hint: Type 138.67 × π and round to one decimal place.

guided_steps.say: Check: big cone 144π ≈ 452.4, small cone 5.33π ≈ 16.8; 452.4 − 16.8 ≈ 435.6 cm³.

problem_bank.bronze_description: Put numbers straight into a volume or surface-area formula for a cube, cuboid, prism or cylinder.
problem_bank.silver_description: Curved shapes and reverse problems: handle the π, the one-third or four-thirds factor, or rearrange to find a missing length.
problem_bank.gold_description: Work backwards from a volume given in terms of π, or combine and subtract solids like frustums and compound shapes.

worked_examples.question: Find the volume of a cuboid 8 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm.
Find the volume of a cone with radius 6 cm and height 10 cm to 1 d.p.
Find the surface area of a sphere with radius 5 cm to 1 d.p.

bronze.title: Bronze: put numbers into the formula
steps: Name the solid, then pick its formula. A cuboid is length × width × height, a prism is cross-section area × length, a cylinder is \(\pi r^2 h\).
Substitute the numbers and multiply carefully, squaring or cubing where the formula says so.
For surface area add up every face: a cube has 6 equal faces, a cuboid has three pairs. Give volume in cm³ and area in cm².

example.question: Find the volume of a cuboid 5 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm.

silver.title: Silver: curved shapes and reverse problems
steps: Now the formula carries a \(\pi\) and often a fraction: cone \(\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\), sphere \(\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), hemisphere two thirds of \(\pi r^3\).
Work out the number in front of \(\pi\) first, then multiply by \(\pi\) at the end and round as asked.
For a reverse problem (a volume is given, find a length) rearrange the formula first, for example \(h = V \div (\pi r^2)\).

example.question: Find the volume of a cone with radius 3 cm and height 8 cm to 1 d.p.

gold.title: Gold: work backwards and combine solids
steps: When a volume is given as a multiple of \(\pi\) (like \(288\pi\)), cancel the \(\pi\) on both sides, rearrange, then take a square or cube root to find the length.
For compound solids work out each part separately and add them; for a frustum, subtract the small cone from the large one.
Keep \(\pi\) as a symbol while you can, and only turn it into a decimal at the final step.

example.question: A sphere has volume 36π cm³. Find the radius.

opener.label: Before any formula
opener.display:
A box is 3 cm long, 2 cm wide and 2 cm tall.
You fill it with 1 cm sugar cubes.

steps.pre: The bottom layer is 3 long and 2 wide. How many cubes cover it?
steps.hint: Three rows of two, or two rows of three.
steps.say: No formula needed. Picture the bottom layer of cubes first.

steps.pre: The box is 2 cubes tall, so how many cubes in total?
steps.say: Now stack the layers up to the top.

You just found the volume: 12 cm³. Counting one layer then stacking it is exactly length × width × height, \(3 \times 2 \times 2 = 12\). Every volume formula is this same idea of filling space, whether the shape is a box, a cylinder or a sphere.

bronze.display: Find the volume of a cuboid 5 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm.
bronze.label: Together: your first one

steps.say: Volume of a cuboid is length × width × height. Just multiply the three numbers.
Now multiply by the height of 2.

steps.done: That returns the length 5 cm, so 40 cm³ is right.

silver.display: Find the volume of a cone with radius 3 cm and height 8 cm to 1 d.p.
silver.label: Together: the silver move

steps.say: A cone brings in two new things: a \(\pi\) and a factor of one third. Volume = \(\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\). Start with r².
A cone is a third of the matching cylinder.

steps.hint: Type 24 × π and round to one decimal place.
steps.done: Gone. The third and the π were the whole point.

gold.display: A sphere has volume \(36\pi\) cm³. Find the radius.
gold.label: Together: the gold move

steps.say: This time the volume is given and we work backwards. \(\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = 36\pi\). Cancel \(\pi\): \(\tfrac{4}{3}r^3 = 36\), so \(r^3 = 36 \times \tfrac{3}{4}\).

steps.done: That gives 36π, the volume we started with, so r = 3 cm.
